About: a rolling wheel meets a step corner

Source

Concept
A rolling disc meets the sharp corner of a raised step in a brief sticking impact, then pivots about the corner. Whether it climbs, and at what launch speed, is the question the inquiry settles.
Model
rolls without slipping (ω = v/R); the strike is sticking, no bounce; the corner grip holds through the pivot
Serves
JEE / NCERT rigid-body rotation: moment of inertia, angular momentum about a point, impulsive torque, energy in an inelastic collision.
Inquiry
Which quantity survives the impact, how the spin just after compares with the spin just before, how the energy books balance across the strike, and how the threshold speed depends on the step height.
Misconception
Addressed in card 3: the student commits to a plausible energy-balance prediction, then launches the wheel at exactly that speed to test it.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealFive gated cards each commit a prediction before the answer-bearing readout or mgh line is unveiled.
Target the misconceptionCard 3 has the student launch the wheel at their own predicted threshold speed and watch what it does.
Invariant made visibleThe strike ledger tracks L about the corner alongside the energy bars, so the student sees for themselves which quantities the impact moves.
Operational numbersEvery readout is a kernel number from the single collision computation; the spoke's rate matches the ω readouts.
Stable, honest sceneFixed 1.2 m × 0.6 m frame, real SI units, slow-motion at the corner labelled explicitly.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Across the strike

The wheel rolls towards the step at 1.2 m s⁻¹ with the height set to 0.10 m. During the brief sticking impact at the corner, before predicting the outcome, decide which quantity is unchanged across the impact.

2 · Spin after sticking

The spoke lets you compare the spin just before and just after the impact. Before pressing go, predict how the angular speed just after the wheel sticks to the corner compares with the angular speed of rolling just before.

3 · Naive threshold

A student balances the rolling kinetic energy ¾mv² against mgh for the 0.10 m step and predicts a threshold speed of 1.14 m s⁻¹. Before launching the wheel at exactly that speed, predict what it does.

4 · Fraction vs speed

The readout shows the energy lost in the impact. Before trying a faster launch at the same step height, predict how the fraction of the kinetic energy lost in the collision changes as the launch speed is raised.

5 · Taller step

At height 0.10 m the threshold speed is 1.47 m s⁻¹. For a smooth ramp the needed speed would grow as √h, which predicts 1.80 m s⁻¹ at 0.15 m. Before moving the height slider to 0.15 m, predict the threshold there.

Wheel Meeting a Step

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A uniform wheel of mass 1 kg and radius 0.30 m rolls without slipping toward a step. It meets the sharp corner of the step in one brief impact. You set the launch speed and the step height, and the sim shows what the wheel does next.

What you'll learn

  • How the wheel's spin and energy just after the corner compare with just before.
  • How the launch speed and the step height each affect whether the wheel gets onto the step.
  • How to find the slowest launch that just clears a given step.
The apparatus: a uniform wheel of radius R rolls at speed v toward a step of height h. The amber dot is the corner it will meet. The orange spoke is the painted one. Not to scale.

What's on screen

  • The wheel, with one painted spoke that turns with it.
  • The corner of the step, marked by a dot, and a grid in 0.2 m by 0.1 m cells.
  • The path of the centre, coloured by stage: roll in, pivot arc, fall back, top run. A stage is named in the legend once it has happened.
See itLook at the wheel waiting at the start of its approach. Watch for: the wheel at the left, the step at the right, and the amber dot at the corner.
02

Fixed: m = 1 kg, R = 0.30 m, g = 9.8 m/s². The wheel sticks to the corner with no bounce, and the corner holds it while it pivots. Around the corner the animation runs in slow motion (×0.30), but the readouts use real units.

03

Angular momentum about the corner is unchanged by the strike

The corner exerts a large force for a very short time. That force changes the wheel's linear momentum and its kinetic energy. But the force acts at the corner, so about the corner its moment arm is zero and it exerts no torque there. Gravity's torque is finite, so over a vanishingly short impact it changes nothing. The angular momentum about the corner, Lc, is therefore the same just before and just after.

Just before the strike Lc has two parts: the wheel's own spin, ½mR² × v/R, and the momentum of its centre, mv, acting at a moment arm R − h. The centre moves at height R and the corner sits at height h.

Lc = mv (3R/2 − h). At the defaults, 0.180 + 0.240 = 0.420 kg m²/s.

See itLaunch at 1.20 m/s onto the 0.10 m step. Watch for: Lc reading 0.420 before and 0.420 after, and the word “unchanged” beside the corner.
04

The spin just after the strike is smaller

After the strike the wheel turns about the corner, not about its own centre. The parallel-axis theorem gives its moment of inertia about the corner: Ic = ½mR² + mR² = 3mR²/2, three times the value about its centre.

The same Lc divided by a larger Ic gives a smaller spin:

ω′ = Lc/Ic = ω (1 − 2h/3R), where ω = v/R is the spin before.

At the defaults ω = 4.00 rad/s and ω′ = 3.11 rad/s, a factor 7/9. The factor s = 1 − 2h/3R depends only on the step height: 8/9 at h = 0.05 m, 7/9 at 0.10 m and 2/3 at 0.15 m. Conserving Lc does not conserve ω.

See itLaunch at 1.20 m/s onto the tallest step, 0.15 m. Watch for: ω just before 4.00 rad/s and ω just after 2.67 rad/s, a factor 2/3.
05

The energy that survives the strike decides the climb

A rolling disc has kinetic energy ¾mv²: ½mv² for its centre and ¼mv² for its spin. Since ω′ = sω, the energy just after the strike is s² times the energy before. At the defaults 1.080 J becomes 0.653 J, so 0.427 J is lost in the impact.

The climb needs the centre to rise by h, which costs mgh = 0.980 J. The test is made after the strike: ½Icω′² ≥ mgh, which gives

vmin = √(4gh/3) / s.

Balancing ¾mv² against mgh before the strike gives √(4gh/3) = 1.14 m/s at h = 0.10 m. The true threshold is 1.47 m/s, larger by the factor 1/s = 9/7. A wheel launched at 1.14 m/s falls back.

See itLaunch at 1.14 m/s onto the 0.10 m step, with the energy chart on. Watch for: the wheel pivoting up on the corner, stopping short of the top and falling back.
See itLaunch at 1.50 m/s, just above the true threshold. Watch for: the wheel pivoting over the corner and the label “clears the corner”.
06

The fraction lost depends on the step height, not the speed

The energy before the strike and the energy after it both scale as v². Their ratio, s², contains no v, so the fraction lost is set by geometry alone:

1 − s² = 4h(3R − h) / 9R².

A faster wheel loses more joules but the same share of its energy. Only the step height changes the share: 21.0% at h = 0.05 m, 39.5% at 0.10 m and 55.6% at 0.15 m.

At 2.00 m/s on the 0.10 m step the wheel brings in 3.000 J and loses 1.185 J, the same 39.5% as at 1.20 m/s.

See itLaunch at 2.00 m/s onto the 0.10 m step. Watch for: energy lost reading 1.185 J while the lost fraction reads 0.395.
07

The threshold speed rises faster than √h

In vmin = √(4gh/3) / s, the height enters twice. A taller step needs more energy to climb, and it also destroys a larger share of the energy on the way in. For a smooth ramp the speed needed would grow as √h.

Step height h√(4gh/3)1/svmin
0.05 m0.808 m/s1.1250.909 m/s
0.10 m1.143 m/s1.2861.470 m/s
0.15 m1.400 m/s1.5002.100 m/s

The third column is the loss correction, and it grows with h: 1.125 at 0.05 m but 1.5 at 0.15 m. Scaling the 1.47 m/s at 0.10 m by √h would give 1.80 m/s at 0.15 m. The true threshold there is 2.10 m/s, so the √h rule underestimates the speed that a tall step demands.

See itRaise the step to 0.15 m and launch at 2.20 m/s. Watch for: the threshold speed reading 2.10 m/s, and the 2.20 m/s wheel clearing the corner.
08

Where it matters

  • Wheels at a kerb. In this model a larger wheel meets the same kerb with s closer to 1, so it needs a lower speed. This agrees with the everyday experience that large wheels cope better with kerbs.
  • Sticking collisions at a pivot. A rod or disc that catches on a fixed pin is solved the same way: conserve angular momentum about the pin, then use energy afterwards.
Go deeper

The sim is an idealisation. The wheel is a uniform disc with I = ½mR², it rolls without slipping, and the strike is perfectly sticking. The corner's impulse is the only one taken into account. Real wheels bounce, slip and have their mass spread differently, so a real threshold differs from 1.47 m/s.

09

Summary

In one line. A rolling wheel meets the corner of a step in a brief impact, and the sim lets you set the launch speed and the step height to see whether it climbs.

Key points

  • Angular momentum about the corner, Lc = mv(3R/2 − h), is the same just before and just after the strike.
  • The spin falls by s = 1 − 2h/3R and the kinetic energy by s², so the fraction lost depends only on h.
  • The wheel climbs when the energy after the strike reaches mgh, which means v ≥ √(4gh/3)/s.

Common mix-ups

  • "The corner is rigid, so energy is conserved." Rigid means no bounce, not no loss. The impact destroys 39.5% at the default step.
  • "Angular momentum is conserved, so the spin is unchanged." Lc is conserved, but Ic is three times larger, so ω falls.
  • "Balance ¾mv² against mgh." That uses the energy before the strike, and some of it is lost.

Things to try on your own

  • Set h = 0.05 m and find the lowest launch speed that clears the step.
  • At h = 0.12 m, work out the lost fraction from the formula, then compare with the ledger.
  • At h = 0.10 m, launch at 1.46 m/s and then at 1.47 m/s, and compare.
